items.title: LPG and the Changing Role of the State
items.body:
## What LPG means

- **Liberalisation** — freeing the economy from state controls (industrial delicensing via the **New Industrial Policy, 1991**, ending the *Licence-Permit-Quota Raj*).
- **Privatisation** — reducing the public sector's role through **disinvestment** and private participation.
- **Globalisation** — integrating the domestic economy with the world through trade, investment and technology flows.

> Launched in **1991** under **PM P. V. Narasimha Rao** and **FM Manmohan Singh** in response to the balance-of-payments crisis. *(The economic mechanics of the crisis, FDI and WTO are covered under Economy; here the focus is the governance impact.)*

## From controller to facilitator

- The Indian state shifted from being a **producer and controller** of the economy to a **regulator, facilitator and enabler** — the 'steering, not rowing' model.
- Captured in the slogan **'Minimum Government, Maximum Governance'** and the drive for **Ease of Doing Business** (single-window clearances, deregulation, digitisation).
- Sovereign functions (law and order, defence, justice, core welfare) remain with the state; direct commercial production is progressively ceded to markets.
keyPoints: LPG = Liberalisation (delicensing), Privatisation (disinvestment), Globalisation (world integration).
New Industrial Policy 1991 dismantled the Licence-Permit-Quota Raj.
Reforms launched in 1991 under PM Narasimha Rao and FM Manmohan Singh.
State role shifted from producer/controller to regulator/facilitator ('steering not rowing').
'Minimum Government, Maximum Governance' and Ease of Doing Business express this shift.
items.mnemonic: LPG = the three doors the 1991 reforms opened: License-free (L), Private (P), Global (G).

items.title: The Rise of the Regulatory State
items.body:
## Governance by regulators

As the state withdrew from direct ownership, it created **independent statutory regulators** to govern liberalised markets at arm's length — the hallmark of the **'regulatory state'**.

| Regulator | Sector | Enabling law |
|---|---|---|
| **SEBI** | Securities market | SEBI Act, 1992 |
| **TRAI** | Telecom | TRAI Act, 1997 |
| **IRDAI** | Insurance | IRDA Act, 1999 |
| **CCI** | Competition/anti-trust | Competition Act, 2002 |

## Public sector reconfiguration

- **Disinvestment** — government sells equity in PSUs (minority sale = retain control; strategic sale = transfer management). Handled by **DIPAM**.
- Strong PSUs granted autonomy via **Maharatna / Navratna / Miniratna** status.
- The **MRTP Act** was replaced by the modern **Competition Act, 2002** (CCI), signalling a move from *controlling monopolies* to *promoting competition*.
keyPoints: Liberalisation created independent regulators to govern markets at arm's length ('regulatory state').
SEBI (1992) — securities; TRAI (1997) — telecom; IRDAI (1999) — insurance; CCI (2002 Act) — competition.
Disinvestment (via DIPAM) dilutes government equity in PSUs — minority vs strategic sale.
Maharatna/Navratna status grants operational and financial autonomy to strong PSUs.
MRTP Act replaced by the Competition Act, 2002 — from curbing monopoly to promoting competition.

items.title: Impact on Federalism
items.body:
## Competitive federalism

- Liberalisation gave **states a direct stake** in economic policy: they now compete to attract **investment and FDI** through incentives, single-window clearances and investor summits.
- This **competitive federalism** is institutionalised in rankings such as the **Ease of Doing Business / Business Reforms Action Plan** (states ranked on reform implementation).

## Cooperative federalism

- The reforms era also built **cooperative-federalism** forums where the Centre and states decide jointly:

| Body | Basis | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **NITI Aayog** | Executive resolution, 2015 | Policy think-tank; cooperative & competitive federalism (replaced Planning Commission) |
| **GST Council** | Art 279A (101st Amdt, 2016) | Joint decisions on indirect taxes |
| **Inter-State Council** | Art 263 | Centre-state coordination |

- Net effect: states became **more**, not less, relevant — as economic actors and policy partners.
keyPoints: Liberalisation empowered states as economic actors competing for investment ('competitive federalism').
Institutionalised via Ease of Doing Business / Business Reforms Action Plan state rankings.
NITI Aayog (2015) replaced the Planning Commission and promotes cooperative & competitive federalism.
GST Council (Art 279A) is a joint Centre-state fiscal decision-making body.
States became more relevant, not less, under reforms.

items.title: Welfare State, Civil Society & Accountability
items.body:
## The reconfigured welfare state

- Welfare was **not abolished** but **reconfigured** — from broad, universal price subsidies toward **targeted delivery**.
- The **JAM trinity** — **J**an Dhan (bank accounts) + **A**adhaar (identity) + **M**obile — is the digital backbone for **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)**, cutting leakage and ghost beneficiaries.
- Rights-based welfare also expanded in this era (e.g. **MGNREGA 2005**, **RTE 2009**), showing the state balancing markets with social protection.

## Civil society and accountability

- A retreating state and rising rights-consciousness enlarged the space for **NGOs, civil society and Public Interest Litigation (PIL)**.
- Transparency and accountability tools grew: the **RTI Act, 2005**, **social audit** (mandated under MGNREGA), and citizen charters (**Sevottam**).
keyPoints: Welfare was reconfigured, not abolished — from universal subsidy to targeted delivery.
JAM trinity = Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + Mobile, powering Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT).
Rights-based welfare expanded alongside markets (MGNREGA 2005, RTE 2009).
Liberalisation era saw growth of NGOs, civil society and PIL.
Accountability tools grew: RTI Act 2005, social audit, citizen charters (Sevottam).

items.title: Social Impact, Sovereignty & Critiques
items.body:
## Social impact

- **Positives** — expansion of the middle class, consumer choice, services and IT boom, poverty reduction over the long run.
- **Concerns** — **rising inequality**, **'jobless growth'** (output rising faster than employment), a large **informal sector**, and widening **urban-rural and regional divides**.

## Globalisation and sovereignty

- Integration with global institutions (e.g. the **WTO**) can **constrain domestic policy space** — a debate about *conditioned* rather than *lost* sovereignty.
- The state retains full constitutional authority and negotiates trade-offs (e.g. defending **agri subsidies / public stockholding** while opening other sectors).

## Enduring debates

- **State vs market** — how far the state should retreat.
- **Agrarian distress** and precarity of informal workers as costs of reform.
- Reforms are widely seen as *irreversible in direction*, with debate focused on their *pace, sequencing and inclusiveness*.
keyPoints: Gains: middle-class expansion, consumer choice, services/IT growth, long-run poverty decline.
Costs: rising inequality, jobless growth, large informal sector, urban-rural/regional divides.
Globalisation conditions (not eliminates) sovereignty — 'policy space' shrinks under treaty commitments.
State keeps constitutional authority and negotiates trade-offs (e.g. agri subsidies at WTO).
Core debate is now pace, sequencing and inclusiveness of reform, not its direction.

items.title: PYQ Precision — WTO, FEMA, FRBM & Industrial Policy
items.body:
## Globalisation milestones

- India was a **founder member of the WTO** (began **1 Jan 1995**, from GATT 1947; Uruguay Round/Marrakesh 1994).
- **FERA 1973 -> FEMA 1999**: forex violations shifted from criminal to civil; a liberalisation hallmark.

## Fiscal discipline

- **FRBM Act 2003** — statutory framework setting fiscal/revenue-deficit reduction targets; N.K. Singh review committee proposed a debt-to-GDP anchor.

## New Industrial Policy 1991

- Abolished **industrial licensing** for most industries; cut public-sector-reserved industries (**17 -> 8**, later only atomic energy & railways core).
- **PSU Ratna grades** (Navratna 1997, Maharatna 2010, Miniratna) came LATER — autonomy tiers, not part of the 1991 policy.
- **Disinvestment** via **DIPAM**; **National Monetisation Pipeline (2021)**; Air India -> Tata (2022); LIC IPO (2022).
keyPoints: India was a founder member of the WTO (began 1 Jan 1995 from GATT).
FERA 1973 was replaced by FEMA 1999 (forex violations became civil, not criminal).
FRBM Act 2003 sets statutory fiscal-discipline/deficit-reduction targets.
New Industrial Policy 1991 abolished licensing and cut reserved industries from 17 to 8.
PSU Ratna grades (Navratna 1997, Maharatna 2010) came after 1991; disinvestment is run by DIPAM.
items.source: UPSC 2011/2019 Prelims; WTO; FERA/FEMA; FRBM Act 2003; New Industrial Policy 1991

items.title: Wealth Concentration (DPSP) & Gandhism–Marxism
items.body:
**Concentration of wealth:** **Article 39(b) & (c)** of the Directive Principles requires that material resources serve the **common good** and that the economic system **not concentrate wealth and means of production to the common detriment** — the ideological counterweight to unregulated LPG-era markets.

**Gandhism & Marxism:** both ideologies converge on the ideal of an eventual **stateless society** — Gandhi through self-regulating village communities and trusteeship, Marx through the withering away of the state.
keyPoints: Article 39(b) & (c) direct that resources serve the common good and wealth not be concentrated to the common detriment.
Gandhism and Marxism both envisage an eventual stateless society.
